question.text: Do domestic producers make goods that buyers can use in place of the covered imports, so that dearer imports send buyers to them?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-014 (illustrative figures), A-17: lower imports are not offset by capital flows or other adjustments within the medium horizon.

question.text: When the country buys fewer imports, foreigners earn less of its currency. Through the exchange rate (the currency rises against what it would otherwise be) this makes the country's exports dearer abroad, so export industries sell less: that is the mechanism, not an offset to it. Over the medium run, will this chain operate, rather than being cancelled by foreigners investing or lending more in the country?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-014 (illustrative figures), A-6: importers know the allocation formula during the window and can finance and store extra imports.

question.text: Can the buyers or importers buy ahead of the effective date, by storing the good or placing orders early?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-014 (illustrative figures), A-8: importing blends and syrups with 65% sugar or less is technically and commercially workable for some users.

question.text: For some of the actors bound by the measure, will reshaping goods so that they fall outside the measure's definitions cost less than the measure would cost them?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-014 (illustrative figures), A-22: the customs budget is raised to cover inspection of bulk shipments and the register of quota rights.

source_sentences: Imports of raw and refined sugar, and of mixtures containing more than 65% sugar by weight, are limited to 350,000 tonnes a year from the effective date, and importers are bound by the limit.
The quota has no expiry, but parliament must review it after five years.
The annual quota is divided into shares that are allocated free to importers, in proportion to each importer's sugar imports over the 36 months before the effective date.
Shares are permanent and may be sold or leased; transfers are registered with customs.
The customs service enforces the quota.
Imports without quota rights are seized and fined three times their value.
Bulk cargo may enter only through Quellport and Varo, where every shipment is inspected; the land crossing at Varnholt is checked by sample.
Enforcement is funded from the general budget.

context: The Republic of Calvar (about 20 million people) uses about 1.2 million tonnes of sugar a year.
Domestic farmers grow sugar beet, which four beet factories turn into about 450,000 tonnes of white sugar.
The rest, about 750,000 tonnes, is imported, mostly as raw cane sugar that two refineries at the ports of Quellport and Varo refine.
World sugar prices have been below the cost of most Calvarian beet growers for years.
Corn syrup is made from domestic corn by two wet mills.

Calvar's only land neighbor, Ostria, has no sugar quota; the border town of Varnholt (150,000 people) is 20 minutes from Ostrian supermarkets, but Calvar's main cities are 200 km or more from the border.
The bill was introduced with government backing nine months before the effective date and passed four months later.
